original_value: AbstractWe introduce a new type of distributional constraints called ratio constraints, which explicitly specify the required balance among schools in two-sided matching. Since ratio constraints do not belong to the known well-behaved class of constraints called M-convex set, developing a fair and strategyproof mechanism that can handle them is challenging. We develop a novel mechanism called quota reduction deferred acceptance (QRDA), which repeatedly applies the standard DA by sequentially reducing artificially introduced maximum quotas. As well as being fair and strategyproof, QRDA always yields a weakly better matching for students compared to a baseline mechanism called artificial cap deferred acceptance (ACDA), which uses predetermined artificial maximum quotas. Finally, we experimentally show that, in terms of student welfare and nonwastefulness, QRDA outperforms ACDA and another fair and strategyproof mechanism called Extended Seat Deferred Acceptance (ESDA), in which ratio constraints are transformed into minimum and maximum quotas.

result.paraphrase: We introduce a new class of distributional constraints, ratio constraints, that explicitly set the needed balance among schools in two-sided matching. Because ratio constraints are not part of the known well-behaved family of constraints known as M-convex sets, it is difficult to design a fair and strategyproof mechanism that can accommodate them. To address this, we develop a new mechanism, quota reduction deferred acceptance (QRDA), which repeatedly runs the standard DA while sequentially lowering artificially introduced maximum quotas. In addition to being fair and strategyproof, QRDA always produces a weakly better student matching than the baseline artificial cap deferred acceptance (ACDA), which relies on preset artificial maximum quotas. Finally, our experiments show that QRDA outperforms ACDA and another fair and strategyproof mechanism, Extended Seat Deferred Acceptance (ESDA), where ratio constraints are converted into minimum and maximum quotas, in both student welfare and nonwastefulness.
